analysis.one_liner: Caps prices drug makers can charge the VA and safety-net clinics for prescriptions.
analysis.headline: The House passed the bill by voice vote on September 22, 1992, but the Senate Finance Committee never acted, and the bill died when the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would force drug manufacturers to make their drugs available for federal purchase at capped prices: no more than 76 percent of the average private-market price for drugs bought by the Department of Veterans Affairs, with an extra discount if prices rise faster than inflation. It would also give community health centers, HIV drug programs, family planning clinics, hemophilia centers, and certain public hospitals the right to buy drugs at the same discounted level Medicaid gets. In exchange, it would keep those discounted government prices out of the formula that sets drug makers' Medicaid rebate bills.
analysis.who_benefits: Veterans who get prescriptions through the VA, and patients of safety-net providers — federally qualified health centers, Ryan White HIV programs, family planning clinics, hemophilia treatment centers, and certain hospitals that serve low-income patients — who would pay less for prescription drugs because their providers buy at government-negotiated discounts.

how_it_helps.text: Caps the price of covered drugs bought by the VA at no more than 76 percent of the non-federal average manufacturer price, a discount of at least 24 percent off private-market prices, with an additional discount whenever prices rise faster than the Consumer Price Index.
Requires manufacturers to list their covered drugs on the Federal Supply Schedule so the government can actually buy them at the capped price, effective for agreements beginning in 1993.

Extends discounted prices to covered entities — federally qualified health centers, Ryan White HIV drug programs, family planning projects, hemophilia centers, and certain disproportionate-share hospitals — set at the average manufacturer price minus the Medicaid rebate percentage.
Requires quarterly price reports from manufacturers and authorizes the VA to audit manufacturers and wholesalers to verify prices.
Directs HHS to study extending the same discounts to mental health, substance abuse, tuberculosis, sexually transmitted disease, and maternal and child health providers.

analysis.who_pays: Prescription drug manufacturers, who would take lower revenue on federal and safety-net sales. The bill partially offsets that by excluding government-negotiated prices from the Medicaid 'best price' calculation, which otherwise would have increased the rebates manufacturers owe states on Medicaid sales.

drawbacks.text: Excludes prices charged to the VA, Indian Health Service, Federal Supply Schedule buyers, and covered entities from the Medicaid 'best price' formula, shielding manufacturers from the larger Medicaid rebates those deep discounts would otherwise trigger — a trade-off that reduces Medicaid savings.
Reduces the minimum Medicaid rebate percentage on a declining schedule, from 15.7 percent of average manufacturer price for quarters in late 1992 down to 15.1 percent after 1995.

Covered entities must submit to audits at the request of manufacturers themselves, and if found in violation of the no-resale or no-duplicate-rebate rules they owe the manufacturer the full value of the discount.

Manufacturers' price reports and audit data obtained by the VA would remain confidential from the public, with review limited to the Comptroller General, limiting transparency about how the discounts compare across drugs.

The good-faith objection: the design was a negotiated compromise — the price caps came bundled with best-price relief, so industry gave up revenue on federal sales in exchange for protecting its Medicaid rebate exposure on everything else.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill delivers a large, concrete benefit to veterans and low-income clinic patients — at least 24 percent off drug prices plus inflation protection — paid for by manufacturers on those specific sales. The main cost to the public is the best-price exclusion: the country buys the discounts partly by giving up some future Medicaid rebate leverage, which is why the bill was shaped this way. On balance the discounts to patients are real and direct, and the design flaw worth noting is confidentiality of the price data, which would make the program hard for outsiders to scrutinize.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it by voice vote under suspension of the rules — a fast-track procedure for bills members treat as noncontroversial — but the Senate Finance Committee, which received it on October 8, 1992, never voted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced on July 15, 1991 by Rep. G.V. (Sonny) Montgomery of Mississippi and referred to the House Energy and Commerce and Veterans' Affairs committees.
The bill drew 105 cosponsors, 72 Democrats and 33 Republicans.
The Veterans' Affairs Committee reported it in November 1991, and after further hearings and markups the Energy and Commerce Committee reported it as amended on September 22, 1992.
The House passed the bill by voice vote on September 22, 1992, on a motion to suspend the rules and pass as amended.
The Senate received the bill on September 24, 1992 and referred it to the Finance Committee on October 8, 1992, where no further action was taken before the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Drug manufacturers came out ahead: the mandatory price caps on VA and safety-net sales, and the required Federal Supply Schedule listings, never took effect. Veterans and safety-net clinic patients got no discounts from this bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Drug makers avoided the price caps

for.name: Rep. G.V. (Sonny) Montgomery
for.role: Chairman, House Committee on Veterans' Affairs
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill, reported it from the Veterans' Affairs Committee, and moved on the House floor to suspend the rules and pass it.

for.name: House Committee on Energy and Commerce
for.what_they_did: Held hearings and markups and reported the bill as amended on September 22, 1992, clearing it for a House vote.

for.name: 105 House cosponsors (72 D, 33 R)
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, giving the bill bipartisan backing across both parties.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.what_they_did: Received the bill and referred it on October 8, 1992, then took no further action; the bill died there when the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan — 72 Democrats and 33 Republicans cosponsored, and the House passed it by voice vote with no recorded opposition — so the obstacle was the Senate's inaction, not a party split.

industries.note: The bill would cap prices on federal and safety-net sales at 76 percent of the average private price with inflation-linked discounts, cutting manufacturer revenue on those sales. But it also excludes those government prices from the Medicaid best-price formula, sparing manufacturers from bigger Medicaid rebates — a negotiated trade.

industries.industry: Safety-net clinics and hospitals (community health centers, HIV drug programs, family planning clinics, hemophilia centers, disproportionate-share hospitals)
industries.note: These providers would buy outpatient drugs at the average manufacturer price minus the Medicaid rebate percentage, lowering what their largely low-income patients pay. In return they accept audit and resale restrictions and liability for the discount if they break the rules.

industries.industry: VA pharmacy purchasing and federal supply contracting
industries.note: The bill requires manufacturers to list covered drugs on the Federal Supply Schedule and report prices quarterly, giving the VA guaranteed access at capped prices and audit authority over manufacturers and wholesalers.
